narrative: The model estimated a 52.4% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—slightly more likely than not—and that estimate led to denial of your law school admission. The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That contrast pushed the prediction toward failure more than any other factor. Your LSAT score of 39 was the second most influential factor; it is above the accepted-student average of about 37.2, so it pushed toward passing, but it was not enough to offset the academic-standing signals. The third factor was your first-year class standing: again the lowest decile, compared with an accepted average near the sixth decile, which also pushed toward failure. Together, the two class-standing indicators outweighed the positive LSAT signal. The prediction is a probability, not a certainty, so this is not a judgment that you cannot succeed. Next, ask admissions for feedback, provide an addendum if there are circumstances explaining your early rankings, strengthen your record with additional academic or professional evidence, and consider retaking the LSAT to create a clearer positive signal. Reapply only when you can show stronger evidence of bar-readiness.
